title: Decimals for Grade 4: Tenths and Hundredths Made Simple + Free Quiz
meta_title: Decimals Grade 4: Tenths and Hundredths Guide
meta_desc: Teach decimals grade 4 tenths and hundredths the clear way: place value, fraction links, number lines and money, with a free 8-question quiz to test it.
excerpt: A decimal is just a tidy way to write a fraction with a denominator of 10 or 100. Here is how I introduce tenths and hundredths to Grade 4, using money and a ruler, plus a quick quiz to check it stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 4 child a ₹10 note and a single one-rupee coin and ask, ‘how do we write one rupee as part of ten?’ The pause you get is the exact gap that decimals fill. This is where decimals grade 4 tenths and hundredths begins — not with rules to memorise, but with the simple idea that a decimal is another way to write a fraction whose denominator is 10 or 100. Get that one sentence to land and the rest of the topic stops feeling like a new language.

In my experience teaching nine-year-olds, the mistake is rushing to the decimal point before the fraction is solid. A child who already knows that 7 tenths means 7 out of 10 equal parts will read 0.7 in seconds. A child who has only seen the dot will guess. So we start with fractions the child already trusts, then show the shorter way to write them.

A decimal is a fraction in disguise

Cut a strip of paper into ten equal pieces. Three shaded pieces are 3 tenths — the fraction 3/10. The decimal way to write that same amount is 0.3. Nothing has changed except the notation. Now cut a square into a 10-by-10 grid so it has 100 tiny cells. One shaded cell is 1 hundredth, or 1/100, or 0.01.

The link is the whole point of Grade 4 decimals, so say it out loud often: 7/10 is 0.7, and 45/100 is 0.45. When children see the fraction and the decimal side by side enough times, the translation becomes automatic.

The decimal point and place value

To the LEFT of the decimal point we have whole numbers — ones, tens, hundreds — exactly as before. The decimal point is a marker that says ‘the whole part ends here’. To the RIGHT come the parts smaller than one: the first place is tenths, the second place is hundredths.

Take the number 3.46. The 3 is three wholes. The 4 sits in the tenths place, so it means 4 tenths. The 6 sits in the hundredths place, so it means 6 hundredths. Read together: three and forty-six hundredths. That reading — ‘and’ for the point, then the parts — is worth drilling.

Reading and writing decimals

Two habits prevent most errors here.

  • Say the place, not the digits. 0.24 is ‘twenty-four hundredths’, never ‘zero point two four’ when you are first building meaning. The proper name keeps the value in view.
  • Watch the zeros. 0.4 and 0.04 look similar and mean very different things: four tenths versus four hundredths. A missing or extra zero shifts the whole value.

Here is a counter-intuitive one that surprises children: 0.5 and 0.50 are the same amount. Five tenths equals fifty hundredths — the extra zero on the right adds nothing. That is genuinely useful later when comparing decimals, so it is worth showing early with the 10-by-10 grid.

Money and a ruler make it real

Rupees and paise are decimals children already half-know. ₹3.75 is three rupees and 75 paise, which is 75 hundredths of a rupee because 100 paise make one rupee. Ask a child to write ₹2 and 5 paise and watch whether they write 2.05 or the wrong 2.5 — that single question exposes whether the hundredths place is understood.

Measurement is the other honest context. On a ruler, one centimetre split into ten equal marks gives millimetres, so 3 cm and 4 mm is 3.4 cm. Length, money, and the paper grid together give three pictures of the same idea, which is far stronger than one.

Decimals on a number line

Draw a line from 0 to 1 and mark ten equal steps. Each step is one tenth: 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and so on up to 1.0. Placing 0.7 becomes a simple count of seven steps. To reach hundredths, zoom in: take the gap between 0.3 and 0.4 and split THAT into ten, and each little step is a hundredth — 0.31, 0.32, and onward.

The number line also settles comparing decimals painlessly: whichever decimal sits further right is larger. To compare 0.4 and 0.36 without a line, line up the places — 0.4 is 0.40, which is 40 hundredths, and 40 is more than 36, so 0.4 > 0.36. Children who compare digit-by-digit without lining up the places often decide 0.36 is bigger because it ‘has more digits’. Catch that early.

A simple order to teach it

Tenths first, and only tenths, until reading and writing them is effortless. Then hundredths on the grid. Then the fraction-to-decimal link both ways. Then the number line for placing and comparing. Money can thread through all of it because children care about money. I would not touch adding or subtracting decimals yet — that is next year’s work, and forcing it now just muddies the place-value idea you worked to build.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The free quiz below covers exactly what we walked through: tenths and hundredths, the fraction link, reading decimals, the number line, and simple comparing. Let your child attempt all eight, then read the explanations together for any misses. When they want longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Decimals Quiz: Tenths and Hundredths
quiz.intro: Eight questions on tenths, hundredths, the fraction link, the number line and comparing. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: How do you write the fraction 7/10 as a decimal?
questions.explanation: 7/10 is seven tenths, so the 7 goes in the first place after the point: 0.7.

questions.q: In the number 3.46, which digit is in the hundredths place?
questions.explanation: The first place after the point is tenths (4) and the second place is hundredths, so 6 is in the hundredths place.

questions.q: What is 25/100 written as a decimal?
questions.explanation: 25/100 is twenty-five hundredths, which fills two places after the point: 0.25.

questions.q: Which decimal is the same amount as 0.5?
questions.explanation: Five tenths equals fifty hundredths, so 0.5 and 0.50 are the same amount.

questions.q: How is ₹3 and 75 paise written using a decimal?
questions.explanation: 100 paise make one rupee, so 75 paise is 75 hundredths: ₹3.75.
0.4 is 0.40, which is 40 hundredths, and 40 is more than 36, so 0.4 is larger.

questions.q: On a number line from 0 to 1 split into ten equal steps, where is 0.7?
questions.explanation: Each step is one tenth, so 0.7 is seven steps from 0.

questions.q: What is three hundredths written as a decimal?
questions.explanation: Three hundredths puts the 3 in the second place after the point, with a zero holding the tenths place: 0.03.

faq.q: What are tenths and hundredths in Grade 4?
faq.a: They are the first two places to the right of the decimal point. A tenth is one of ten equal parts of a whole (1/10 = 0.1), and a hundredth is one of a hundred equal parts (1/100 = 0.01). Grade 4 is usually where decimals appear formally.

faq.q: How do I explain a decimal to my child?
faq.a: Say it is a shorter way to write a fraction with a denominator of 10 or 100. Show 3/10 and 0.3 as the same shaded strip, and 45/100 and 0.45 as the same shaded grid, so the notation feels like a translation rather than a new idea.

Five tenths equals fifty hundredths — a 10-by-10 grid shows five full columns is the same shaded area as fifty small cells. A zero added on the far right of a decimal does not change its value, which helps a lot when comparing decimals.

faq.q: Should Grade 4 learn to add and subtract decimals?
faq.a: Not in depth yet. Grade 4 focuses on understanding place value, reading and writing decimals, the fraction link, the number line and simple comparing. Operations with decimals are usually built in the next grade once the place-value idea is secure.
